passage:
Sunday. Lalit scrolled past a headline in the hostel mess: "Coffee drinkers live longer, big study finds." He read it twice, then showed Santosh. "Bro, coffee is basically medicine."
Wednesday. Lalit was now drinking cup after cup of filter coffee and had stopped his evening run, because the coffee "was doing the work". Santosh raised an eyebrow. "Maybe coffee people just have jobs and money and friends to go to cafés with. Or maybe people who get ill stop drinking coffee."
"Nah, the study is huge," Lalit said.
The next Monday. Lalit, jittery and short on sleep, finally opened the actual article. Near the bottom: "The study shows a link; it does not show that coffee causes longer life." He sighed, put on his running shoes, and went back to his one morning cup.

qa.q: What did the line near the bottom of the article say?
qa.a: "The study shows a link; it does not show that coffee causes longer life."

qa.q: Why did the headline convince Lalit so quickly?
qa.a: It was short, confident and said 'big study', so Lalit read it as coffee making people live longer and liked the idea of an easy shortcut.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Lalit swapped his evening run for coffee because of a headline; reading the full article and seeing it showed only a link sent him back to running.

qa.q: How does Santosh see the coffee study?
qa.a: Santosh thinks something else could explain it, like coffee drinkers having money and friends, or ill people giving up coffee.

grounding: It shows a student turning a headline about coffee drinkers into the belief that coffee itself causes longer life, until hidden factors come up.

passage:
Another coffee, Ujjwal? Sit. Let Parveen aunty tell you something. When I was nineteen, in my second year at Aligarh, a magazine in the reading room said coffee drinkers live longer. I had never liked coffee, but I started drinking it with every meal. I told my roommates it was for my health. I really believed each cup was adding years to my life.
Then my statistics professor brought that same article to class. He asked us, "Who drinks coffee in this country?" People with a bit of money, office jobs, time to sit in coffee houses. People with healthier lives for many reasons. And people who are already unwell often give coffee up. The coffee wasn't the reason; it was riding along with other things. I felt so foolish. So drink your coffee because you like it, not because a headline told you to.

qa.q: Where did Parveen aunty read about coffee drinkers?
qa.a: In a magazine in the reading room, in her second year at Aligarh.

qa.q: Why did Parveen start drinking coffee with every meal though she never liked it?
qa.a: She felt hopeful that each cup was adding years to her life, so the headline turned a link into a reason to change her habits.

qa.q: What question did the professor ask, and why does it help?
qa.a: He asked who drinks coffee in the country, which brought out hidden factors like money, office jobs and free time that could explain longer lives.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal take this story from Parveen aunty?
qa.a: Ujjwal might feel gently teased about the coffee, but also see that she is sharing her own mistake so he won't trust headlines too quickly.

grounding: It shows a student believing coffee caused longer life after reading a headline, before learning hidden factors can explain the link.

passage:
Twenty minutes before the inter-college debate, Shalini was still scribbling her opening line on the back of a canteen bill: "Science has proven that coffee makes you live longer." She had seen the headline that morning, "Coffee drinkers outlive non-drinkers", and it had felt like a gift.
Kavitha, her teammate, read it over her shoulder and winced. "Proven? It said coffee drinkers outlive others. That's not the same."
"It's the same thing."
"What if richer people drink more coffee and also see doctors more? Or people who fall ill stop drinking it? Then the coffee isn't doing anything."
Shalini looked at the clock. Twelve minutes. She had no time to find the study, no data pack, only the headline. She crossed out "proven" and wrote "linked", then stared at the word, unconvinced.

qa.q: What did Shalini write her opening line on?
qa.a: The back of a canteen bill.

qa.q: Why does Shalini think 'drinkers outlive non-drinkers' means the same as 'coffee makes you live longer'?
qa.a: Shalini felt pleased because the headline seemed like a gift for her debate, and when two things go together it seems natural that one causes the other, so the difference feels like nitpicking.

qa.q: What could Shalini say in the debate that stays honest?
qa.a: She could say coffee drinkers were found to live longer but that other things, like money or illness, might explain it, so the link isn't proof.

qa.q: What would change if Shalini had time to read the full study?
qa.a: She might find out whether it looked at money or illness, and could build her argument on what it really showed instead of on a headline.

grounding: It shows a student under time pressure treating a coffee-and-long-life headline as proof that coffee is the cause.

passage:
Maria, twenty, was eating toast on the balcony of her Bengaluru PG when the headline popped up on her phone: "Coffee drinkers live longer, huge study finds."
By lunch she had bought a bag of filter coffee powder and a steel tumbler set. By the evening she was on her third cup.
"You hate coffee," Simran said from the doorway.
"I'm learning to like it. It's science. The study had half a million people."
"Did it say why they lived longer?"
"Because of the coffee, obviously."
Simran picked up the phone and scrolled. "It says coffee drinkers in the study also walked more and smoked less."
Maria took the phone back and scrolled up to the headline again. "Yeah, but the big number is about coffee." She poured another cup, grimacing at the bitterness.

qa.q: How many people did Maria say the study had?
qa.a: Half a million people.

qa.q: How does Maria feel about the coffee headline, and what shows it?
qa.a: Maria feels convinced and eager, buying coffee powder by lunch and drinking a third cup by evening, even grimacing at the bitterness, because the huge study sounds like proof.

qa.q: At which moment could Maria think again, and what could she ask?
qa.a: When Simran reads that coffee drinkers also walked more and smoked less; Maria could ask whether those habits, not the coffee, explain the longer lives.

qa.q: How might Simran feel watching Maria drink coffee she dislikes?
qa.a: Simran is probably amused and a little puzzled that Maria forces down a bitter drink because of a headline, especially after pointing out the other habits.

grounding: It shows a student reading that coffee drinkers live longer and believing coffee is the reason, missing hidden third factors.

"Ma, we have to switch Nani from tea to coffee."
"Why, Mahima beti? She's had tea for sixty years."
"I read it. People who drink coffee live longer. It was a big study."

Mahima was quiet for a moment, then: "Still. Coffee people live longer. I read it."

qa.a: Mahima could look up whether the study checked things like walking and eating habits, or whether ill people stop drinking coffee, before deciding coffee is the cause.

qa.a: Sharmila sees other reasons, like morning walks and early meals, and the chance that sick people give up coffee, so to her the link doesn't prove coffee is the cause.

"Gurpreet, listen to this. 'Coffee drinkers live longer, says new study.'" Charu held up the phone across the hostel kitchen. "I'm switching. No more tea for me."
"Longer than whom?"
"Than non-coffee people! It's a study."
"Okay, but who drinks coffee every day? People with desk jobs, people who can afford cafés, people who aren't too unwell to enjoy it."
"So?"
"So maybe the money and the health are what make them live longer. And people who start feeling ill often give up coffee first, which makes non-drinkers look sicker."
Charu paused, mug in hand. "Wait, so the good health could explain the coffee, not the other way round?"
"Sometimes. The headline can't tell you. The study itself might."
"I'll read past the headline, then." She sniffed the mug. "But I'm still drinking this. I like it."
"That's a perfectly good reason."

qa.a: Charu read out 'Coffee drinkers live longer, says new study.'

qa.q: Why did the headline feel convincing enough for Charu to give up tea?
qa.a: Charu felt excited and trusting because a study linked coffee with long life, and that link felt like proof that coffee was the cause.

qa.q: What could Charu do before changing a habit because of a headline?
qa.a: She could read past the headline to see whether the study allowed for things like money, jobs or health, and ask whether illness might change who drinks coffee.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see the coffee claim?
qa.a: Gurpreet sees hidden factors like wealth, desk jobs and health, and even the reverse direction, where people who fall ill stop drinking coffee.

grounding: Shows a student reading a coffee-and-long-life link as cause while a flatmate points to third factors and reversed direction.

passage: Last semester I read a post on the college page: 'Students who sit in the first two rows score higher, study finds.' I'm Noor, and I believed it instantly. The next morning I left my usual corner beside Nazia and marched to the front of the economics lecture. I felt clever and a bit brave. By week three I noticed something. The front-row regulars were the same people who came early, read before class and stayed back with questions. They'd score higher sitting on the roof. Sitting there didn't make me any of those things; I was still copying Nazia's notes late at night. When I told Nazia, Nazia laughed and said, "So the seat was the effect, not the cause." I went back to the corner, and started reading before class instead.

qa.q: Which lecture did Noor move to the front of?
qa.a: Noor moved to the front of the economics lecture.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling on first moving to the front row, and why did the claim seem so convincing?
qa.a: Noor felt clever and a bit brave, because a study linked front seats with higher scores and it seemed obvious that the seat itself would help.

qa.q: What did Noor change in the end, and why is it a better bet?
qa.a: Noor started reading before class, which copies the habit the front-row students actually shared rather than the seat that came with it.

qa.q: How might Nazia have seen Noor's move to the front?
qa.a: Nazia may have found it a little funny and a little lonely to lose a seat partner, and later summed up the lesson: the seat was the effect, not the cause.

grounding: Shows a student believing a headline about front-row seats means the seat causes better scores, until noticing that keen students choose those seats.

Warden's note, postgraduate hostel, 3 November.
Sabina came to the office this morning with a printout and a plan. A headline said people who keep houseplants report less stress, and she wanted permission to put plants on every corridor 'to bring down exam stress'. She was so eager I almost said yes on the spot. Nitin, from the floor committee, asked a good question: who keeps plants? People with spare time, with sunny rooms, people already calm enough to water something every day. Sabina frowned, then laughed. "So calm people get plants, not plants make people calm?" "Maybe both," I said. "The headline can't say." We agreed on a small trial: plants on one corridor only, and a short how-are-you-feeling survey before and after exams on both floors. I'll look at the results with her in January.

qa.q: What did Sabina want to put on every corridor?
qa.a: Sabina wanted to put plants on every corridor.

qa.q: Why did the headline make Sabina so eager?
qa.a: Sabina felt hopeful and keen to ease others' exam stress, and the link between plants and less stress looked like a simple cause she could act on.

qa.q: Why is the one-corridor trial a sensible next step?
qa.a: It compares a corridor with plants to one without during the same exams, which can say more about cause than a headline linking two things.

qa.q: How does Nitin see the houseplant claim?
qa.a: Nitin sees that calm people with time and sunny rooms may be the ones who keep plants, so the link may run the other way.

grounding: Shows a student taking a houseplant-and-stress headline as proof of cause until hidden factors and reversed direction are raised.

Read a headline on my phone this morning: "Coffee drinkers live longer, study finds." I'm Lalremsiami, and I don't even like coffee, but I bought two cups at the canteen today. If it makes you live longer, why not?
Showed Shreya at lunch. She's a biology student. She asked, "Who drinks coffee in that study?" I didn't know. She read the article. People who drank coffee were also more likely to have office jobs, more money, better healthcare. "Maybe it's those things," she said. "Or maybe people who are already sick stop drinking coffee, so the healthy ones look like coffee drinkers."
I felt silly. The headline didn't say coffee causes anything. It said coffee drinkers live longer. Different thing.
Going back to tea tomorrow.

qa.a: Who the people in the study were and what else they had in common, or whether the direction could be reversed.

In their shared flat in Addis Ababa, Abebe read the headline aloud from his phone: "Coffee drinkers live longer, study finds." He looked at the clay coffee pot on the stove with new respect. "I'm doubling my coffee. It's basically medicine."
Javier, his flatmate from the exchange programme, was frying eggs. "Who drinks coffee every day, though?"
"Everyone. My grandparents drank it three times a day their whole lives."
"Your grandparents also walked to the market every morning, sat with neighbours for hours and had steady work. People who have time for a long coffee ceremony usually have time, friends, some money. Maybe that's what keeps them going."
Abebe frowned at the headline. The article, when he scrolled down, said "linked with", not "causes".
"So coffee might just come along with the good life," he said slowly.
"Or not. Read the actual study, not the title."
Abebe poured one cup, his usual one, and opened the article properly.

Kashish read it twice, then went straight to the club fair in the atrium and signed up for five: debate, photography, coding, drama and the eco club.
Nazia, a final-year volunteer at the placement cell, found her filling in the fifth form. "Planning to sleep this semester?"
"Didn't you see the study? Clubs get you jobs."

Kashish looked at the five forms. It had felt so clear a minute ago.
"Pick one you actually like," Nazia said. "Then come for the mock interviews on Thursday. Those you can practise."

Rehana Apa,
Quick update from the hostel. Last week I read an article: "Early risers earn more, study of ten thousand people shows." So I've been waking at five every day. Alarm, cold water, the whole thing. I figured if people who earn more wake early, waking early must make you earn more.
It's day six. I'm exhausted by lunch, and I slept through my 2 p.m. lab.
Last night I actually read the study instead of the headline. It said early risers were "more likely" to earn more. Then it said many of them are older, already have steady day jobs, and have kids who wake them up. So maybe a steady job makes you wake early, not the other way round.
I feel a bit stupid. I've gone back to waking at seven, and I'm going to my lab.
Don't tell Ammi about the five a.m. experiment. She'll laugh.
Tanvir

qa.a: Tanvir slept through the 2 p.m. lab.

qa.a: Tanvir felt hopeful and determined, reading the headline as proof that rising early causes people to earn more.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do that other headline readers could copy?
qa.a: Tanvir read the study itself, found 'more likely' and the third factors like steady jobs and kids, and changed course.

qa.q: How might Rehana react to the email?
qa.a: Rehana might smile and feel fond, glad that Tanvir spotted the mistake and went back to sleeping properly.

grounding: Shows a student who reads that early risers earn more and assumes waking early is the cause, until the study reveals third factors and reversed direction.
